prime.problem: Once text starts streaming, the pace it scrolls at decides how long any answer longer than a few sentences takes. Without a clean per-request number you can't compare hosts, and you'll confuse it with server throughput or end-to-end time.
prime.fits: Second metric card. TTFT covered the wait before the first token; this card is the divisor in the writing-time term, tokens ÷ speed. The mechanism cards later explain what sets it.
expect: tokens per second after the first token
prime.goal: Compute writing time from speed and length, and say what a host's output speed number does and doesn't tell you.

attend: Why does the clock start at the first token and not when the request is sent?
How can the card check that Cerebras and DeepInfra did the same job from TTFT, end-to-end time and speed alone?
Why can a server's throughput go up while each user's output speed goes down?
For an 82-token answer, why do Cerebras and Groq feel almost the same despite a 3.7× speed gap?

must: Tokens are generated strictly one after another → the pace per token sets the whole writing time → writing time = tokens ÷ output speed → a 36× faster host writes the same answer 36× faster
Output speed is timed from the first token → queueing and prompt reading are excluded → it isolates the decode pace, which is what hardware, quantization and serving tricks change
Hosts batch many users per chip to raise throughput → each user's share of the chip shrinks → per-request speed falls → compare hosts on per-request speed, not throughput
elevated: Reasoning models are measured on the last 80% of answer chunks → a high speed can sit on top of a long silent think (Gemini 3.8 Flash high: 344 t/s but 22.7 s TTFT) → always read speed next to TTFT
reference: the nine host speeds for gpt-oss-120b (48–1,745 t/s)

compress.prompt: In 3 sentences from memory: define output speed precisely, say how to turn it into writing time, and name the one thing it deliberately excludes. Then write the end-to-end formula and fill it in for 653 tokens at 48 t/s with 0.65 s TTFT.
checklist: tokens per second after the first token, for one request
653 ÷ 48 = 13.6 s, plus 0.65 s ≈ 14.3 s end to end
not the same as a server's throughput

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between output speed and throughput, and why a cheap host can have high throughput but low output speed.
answer: output speed: one request's tokens/s; throughput: all users' tokens/s on the server
packing more users per chip raises throughput
each user then gets a smaller share, so their speed drops

retrieve.q: Using the card's check, show how Cerebras's TTFT (0.50 s), end-to-end time (1.93 s) and speed (1,745 t/s) imply the size of the job.
answer: DeepInfra gives ≈ 2,483, so both hosts did the same ~2.5k-token job

retrieve.q: When is the fastest host by output speed the wrong pick?
answer: short answers: TTFT dominates, so speed barely matters
reasoning models: a long hidden think can dwarf the writing time
the fastest host may cost more or serve lower precision (check fp4/fp8/bf16)

compare.q: Speed and length sit in the same fraction, tokens ÷ speed. Which one do you control for free, which one costs money, and which one did the card show gives the bigger win on the M3?
answer: length: free (prompt wording, max_tokens, thinking off)
speed: costs a host change or hardware
on the M3: 653 → 82 tokens ≈ 7.9× faster; M3 → M3 Max ≈ 3.1×

compare.q: Output speed here and TPOT (time per output token) on a serving dashboard describe the same pace. How are they related, and which one does a server operator trade away to raise throughput?
answer: operators raise batch size to raise throughput
that lengthens TPOT, so each user's output speed falls

predict.q: A host doubles its batch size to cut cost. Predict what happens to its output speed per request and to its throughput, and say whether either change is exactly 2×.
predict.answer: Throughput rises and per-request speed falls, but neither by exactly 2×. While decode is memory-bound, one weight read serves the whole batch, so a bigger batch costs little extra time per step: throughput nearly doubles and each user slows only a little. Once the batch is big enough that compute or KV-cache reads dominate, each step gets noticeably slower and per-user speed drops more.

apply.task: Measure output speed yourself two ways for one ~300-token answer: (1) from Ollama's eval_count ÷ eval_duration, and (2) by timestamping the first and last streamed chunk and using (tokens − 1) ÷ (tlast − tfirst). Then predict the writing time of a 653-token answer from your number and check it with a real run.
apply.done: Both methods agree within about 10%, and your predicted 653-token writing time is within about 10% of the measured one.
apply.hint: On the M3 with qwen3.5:4b the card measured 15.4 t/s, so 653 tokens should take about 42 s.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: what a bigger batch does to per-user speed?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why a reasoning model's high speed can still mean a long wait?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: batching → throughput, or batching → per-user speed?
Which host number would you now look up before choosing a provider, and where?
What do you expect the memory-bandwidth card to say sets this number?
